```{python}
#| include: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from IPython.display import display, HTML

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor":"#F1F5F9", "axes.facecolor":"#F1F5F9",
    "axes.spines.top":False, "axes.spines.right":False,
    "axes.edgecolor":"#CBD5E1", "axes.labelcolor":"#334155",
    "axes.labelsize":12, "xtick.labelsize":10, "ytick.labelsize":10,
    "xtick.color":"#94A3B8", "ytick.color":"#94A3B8",
    "lines.linewidth":2.2, "font.family":"DejaVu Sans",
    "grid.color":"#E2E8F0", "grid.linewidth":0.7,
    "legend.fontsize":10, "legend.framealpha":0.92,
    "legend.edgecolor":"#E2E8F0", "figure.dpi":130,
})

TEAL="#0D9488"; TEAL2="#14B8A6"; ORANGE="#F97316"; GREEN="#22C55E"
NAVY="#1A3A5C"; RED="#EF4444"; GRAY="#94A3B8"; LGRAY="#E2E8F0"

START = "2019-01-01"
END = "2021-12-31"
COVID_START = pd.Timestamp("2020-02-19")
COVID_TROUGH = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-23")
COVID_END = pd.Timestamp("2020-06-30")

USE_LIVE_DATA = False
# Set USE_LIVE_DATA = True if yfinance is installed and internet is available.
# This deck is Python-only either way. The fallback keeps the file easy to render in class.

def make_fallback_data():
    np.random.seed(406)
    dates = pd.date_range(START, END, freq="B")
    rows = []
    price = 100.0
    for d in dates:
        if d < COVID_START:
            mu, sig = 0.00055, 0.0075
        elif d <= COVID_TROUGH:
            mu, sig = -0.020, 0.040
        elif d <= COVID_END:
            mu, sig = 0.006, 0.030
        else:
            mu, sig = 0.00075, 0.012
        r = np.random.normal(mu, sig)
        price *= (1 + r)
        rows.append([d, price])
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Date", "Close"])
    # Force a recognizable COVID crash and rebound shape without needing internet.
    out.loc[out["Date"].between(COVID_START, COVID_TROUGH), "Close"] *= np.linspace(1.00, 0.70, out["Date"].between(COVID_START, COVID_TROUGH).sum())
    out.loc[out["Date"].between(COVID_TROUGH, COVID_END), "Close"] *= np.linspace(0.72, 1.05, out["Date"].between(COVID_TROUGH, COVID_END).sum())
    return out

def load_data():
    if USE_LIVE_DATA:
        try:
            import yfinance as yf
            raw = yf.download("^GSPC", start=START, end="2022-01-01", progress=False, auto_adjust=False)
            if raw is not None and len(raw) > 500:
                close = raw["Adj Close"] if "Adj Close" in raw.columns else raw["Close"]
                if isinstance(close, pd.DataFrame):
                    close = close.iloc[:, 0]
                out = close.reset_index()
                out.columns = ["Date", "Close"]
                out["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(out["Date"])
                return out, "Yahoo Finance: S&P 500 (^GSPC)"
        except Exception:
            pass
    return make_fallback_data(), "Python fallback: S&P 500 style COVID return series"

df, source_name = load_data()
df = df.dropna().sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)
df["Return"] = df["Close"].pct_change()
df["ReturnPct"] = df["Return"] * 100
df["Index100"] = 100 * df["Close"] / df["Close"].iloc[0]
df["RollingMean"] = df["ReturnPct"].rolling(20).mean()
df["RollingVol"] = df["ReturnPct"].rolling(30).std()
df["MA90"] = df["Index100"].rolling(90).mean()
df["Peak"] = df["Index100"].cummax()
df["Drawdown"] = (df["Index100"] / df["Peak"] - 1) * 100

pre = df[df["Date"] < COVID_START].copy()
shock = df[df["Date"].between(COVID_START, COVID_END)].copy()
post = df[df["Date"] > COVID_END].copy()

crash_window = df[df["Date"].between(COVID_START, COVID_TROUGH)].copy()
crash_return = (crash_window["Index100"].iloc[-1] / crash_window["Index100"].iloc[0] - 1) * 100
peak_vol = df["RollingVol"].max()
peak_vol_date = df.loc[df["RollingVol"].idxmax(), "Date"]
pre_vol = pre["ReturnPct"].std()
shock_vol = shock["ReturnPct"].std()
post_vol = post["ReturnPct"].std()

mean_r = df["ReturnPct"].mean()
std_r = df["ReturnPct"].std()
df["Anomaly"] = (df["ReturnPct"] - mean_r).abs() > 3 * std_r
anomalies = df[df["Anomaly"]].copy()

top_moves = df.dropna(subset=["ReturnPct"]).assign(abs_move=lambda x: x["ReturnPct"].abs()).nlargest(6, "abs_move")
top_table = top_moves[["Date", "ReturnPct", "RollingVol"]].copy()
top_table["Date"] = top_table["Date"].dt.strftime("%b %d, %Y")
top_table["ReturnPct"] = top_table["ReturnPct"].map(lambda x: f"{x:+.2f}%")
top_table["RollingVol"] = top_table["RollingVol"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.2f}%" if pd.notnull(x) else "")
top_table.columns = ["Date", "Daily Return", "30-Day Volatility"]

# Simple forecast from the last 60 trading days. This is intentionally simple for teaching.
forecast_days = 45
last = df.dropna(subset=["Return"]).tail(60)
mu = last["Return"].mean()
sigma = last["Return"].std()
future_dates = pd.bdate_range(df["Date"].max() + pd.offsets.BDay(1), periods=forecast_days)
last_index = df["Index100"].iloc[-1]
base = last_index * np.cumprod(np.repeat(1 + mu, forecast_days))
upper = last_index * np.cumprod(np.repeat(1 + mu + 1.96 * sigma, forecast_days))
lower = last_index * np.cumprod(np.repeat(1 + mu - 1.96 * sigma, forecast_days))
fc = pd.DataFrame({"Date":future_dates, "Forecast":base, "Lower":lower, "Upper":upper})


def metric_grid(items):
    cards = []
    for value, label, color in items:
        cards.append(f"<div class='metric'><div class='n {color}'>{value}</div><div class='l'>{label}</div></div>")
    return "<div class='three-col' style='margin-top:14px;'>" + "".join(cards) + "</div>"

def setup_date_axis(ax):
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    ax.grid(axis="y")

```

## 1. The Business Question

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

A time series is data measured in order over time.

For this presentation, the question is simple:

<div class="dark">
<strong>How did COVID-19 change stock market behavior, and what can analytics teams learn from it?</strong>
</div>

We focus on four ideas that are easy to explain:

<div class="two-col" style="gap:10px; margin-top:12px;">
<div class="card card-teal"><strong>Trend</strong><br><span style="font-size:0.85em;">Long-run direction</span></div>
<div class="card card-orange"><strong>Returns</strong><br><span style="font-size:0.85em;">Daily gains or losses</span></div>
<div class="card card-red"><strong>Volatility</strong><br><span style="font-size:0.85em;">Risk and uncertainty</span></div>
<div class="card card-green"><strong>Anomalies</strong><br><span style="font-size:0.85em;">Unusual market days</span></div>
</div>

::: {.info}
Dataset source used in this file: `Python fallback: S&P 500 style COVID return series`. To use live S&P 500 data, set `USE_LIVE_DATA = True` in the first Python chunk.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.3))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12, label="COVID shock window")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Index100"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.3, label="Market index, Jan 2019 = 100")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["MA90"], color=NAVY, linewidth=2.7, label="90-day trend")
ax.axvline(COVID_TROUGH, color=RED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8, label="Crash trough")
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Index value")
ax.set_title("A market index is a time series", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

## 2. Prices Show the Story, Returns Show the Reaction

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

Prices are useful for the big picture, but returns are better for analysis.

<div class="card card-teal" style="margin-bottom:12px;">
<strong>Price</strong><br>
Shows the level of the market. It usually trends over time.
</div>

<div class="card card-orange" style="margin-bottom:12px;">
<strong>Return</strong><br>
Shows the percentage change from one trading day to the next.
</div>

<div class="dark" style="font-size:0.95em;">
Return = (Today's price - Yesterday's price) / Yesterday's price
</div>

::: {.info}
Why it matters: managers, investors, and analysts usually care about returns because returns measure gain, loss, and risk.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.3))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.11)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["ReturnPct"], color=TEAL, linewidth=0.9, alpha=0.85)
ax.axhline(0, color=NAVY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
ax.axvline(COVID_TROUGH, color=RED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8)
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Daily return (%)")
ax.set_title("Daily returns reveal the market reaction", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)

max_gain = df.loc[df["ReturnPct"].idxmax()]
max_loss = df.loc[df["ReturnPct"].idxmin()]
ax.scatter([max_gain["Date"], max_loss["Date"]], [max_gain["ReturnPct"], max_loss["ReturnPct"]], color=[GREEN, RED], s=65, zorder=5, edgecolors="white")
ax.annotate(f"Largest loss\n{max_loss['ReturnPct']:.1f}%", xy=(max_loss["Date"], max_loss["ReturnPct"]), xytext=(COVID_START, max_loss["ReturnPct"]-3), color=RED, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9.5, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=RED))
ax.annotate(f"Largest gain\n{max_gain['ReturnPct']:.1f}%", xy=(max_gain["Date"], max_gain["ReturnPct"]), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2020-07-01"), max_gain["ReturnPct"]+2), color=GREEN, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9.5, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREEN))
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## 3. COVID Created a Clear Market Shock

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

A market shock is a sudden event that changes expectations.

During the COVID period, investors reacted to:

- Lockdowns and uncertainty
- Business closures
- Policy responses
- Vaccine and reopening expectations

```{python}
display(HTML(metric_grid([
    (f"{crash_return:.1f}%", "drop in the crash window", "red"),
    (f"{peak_vol:.1f}%", "peak 30-day daily volatility", "orange"),
    (f"{len(anomalies)}", "extreme return days flagged", "teal"),
])))
```

::: {.warn}
The point is not just that the market fell. The bigger lesson is that the behavior of the time series changed.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12)
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Index100"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.2)
ax.fill_between(mdates.date2num(crash_window["Date"]), crash_window["Index100"].to_numpy(), crash_window["Index100"].iloc[0], color=RED, alpha=0.13)
ax.axvline(COVID_START, color=ORANGE, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6)
ax.axvline(COVID_TROUGH, color=RED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8)
ax.axvline(COVID_END, color=GREEN, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6)
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Index value")
ax.set_title("Crash and rebound around the COVID shock", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.annotate("Shock begins", xy=(COVID_START, df.loc[df["Date"].sub(COVID_START).abs().idxmin(), "Index100"]), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2019-08-01"), df["Index100"].max()*0.95), color=ORANGE, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9.5, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ORANGE))
ax.annotate("Trough", xy=(COVID_TROUGH, df.loc[df["Date"].sub(COVID_TROUGH).abs().idxmin(), "Index100"]), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2020-05-01"), df["Index100"].min()*0.92), color=RED, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9.5, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=RED))
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

## 4. Volatility Clustering: Big Moves Come Together

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

One important time series pattern is volatility clustering.

That means large movements tend to be followed by more large movements.

<div class="card card-red" style="margin-top:12px;">
<strong>Before COVID:</strong> returns were smaller and calmer.<br>
<strong>During COVID:</strong> positive and negative swings happened back to back.
</div>

::: {.info}
This is why risk teams track rolling volatility instead of looking only at average return.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
plot_df = df.dropna(subset=["ReturnPct"])
colors = np.where(plot_df["ReturnPct"] >= 0, GREEN, RED)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
ax.bar(plot_df["Date"], plot_df["ReturnPct"], color=colors, width=2.5, alpha=0.85)
ax.axhline(0, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.0)
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Daily return (%)")
ax.set_title("Green and red bars show daily market swings", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

## 5. Rolling Volatility Measures Risk

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

Rolling volatility calculates the standard deviation of returns over a moving window.

Here we use a 30-trading-day window.

```{python}
display(HTML(metric_grid([
    (f"{pre_vol:.2f}%", "pre-COVID daily volatility", "teal"),
    (f"{shock_vol:.2f}%", "COVID shock volatility", "red"),
    (f"{post_vol:.2f}%", "post-shock volatility", "green"),
])))
```

::: {.dark}
Simple interpretation: the market became less predictable, so the risk of making a wrong forecast increased.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.11, label="COVID shock")
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["RollingVol"], color=RED, linewidth=2.4, label="30-day rolling volatility")
vol_df = df.dropna(subset=["RollingVol"])
ax.fill_between(mdates.date2num(vol_df["Date"]), vol_df["RollingVol"].to_numpy(), color=RED, alpha=0.13)
ax.axvline(peak_vol_date, color=NAVY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6)
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Volatility (% per day)")
ax.set_title("COVID made returns much more volatile", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.annotate(f"Peak volatility\n{peak_vol:.1f}%", xy=(peak_vol_date, peak_vol), xytext=(pd.Timestamp("2020-09-01"), peak_vol*0.75), color=RED, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9.5, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=RED))
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

## 6. Anomaly Detection Finds Extreme Days

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

A simple way to identify unusual days is the 3-sigma rule.

<div class="dark" style="font-size:0.95em;">
Flag a day if |return - average return| > 3 × standard deviation
</div>

This works well for teaching because it is easy to explain:

- Calculate normal behavior
- Draw upper and lower limits
- Flag points outside those limits

::: {.warn}
The red dots are days where the market moved far more than normal.
:::

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
ax.axvspan(COVID_START, COVID_END, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.10)
normal = df[~df["Anomaly"]]
ax.plot(normal["Date"], normal["ReturnPct"], color=TEAL, linewidth=0.85, alpha=0.65, label="Normal day")
ax.scatter(anomalies["Date"], anomalies["ReturnPct"], color=RED, s=60, zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.6, label="Anomaly")
ax.axhline(mean_r + 3 * std_r, color=GRAY, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5, label="3-sigma boundary")
ax.axhline(mean_r - 3 * std_r, color=GRAY, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
ax.axhline(0, color=NAVY, linewidth=0.9, alpha=0.8)
setup_date_axis(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Daily return (%)")
ax.set_title("Anomaly detection on daily returns", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## 7. Biggest Return Days Tell the Crisis Story

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

Extreme days are useful because they turn a long time series into a short list of business events.

Instead of asking people to read hundreds of rows, we highlight the days that need explanation.

::: {.info}
In real stock data, these dates would be matched with news: lockdown announcements, central bank actions, fiscal stimulus, earnings warnings, and vaccine updates.
:::

```{python}
top_table
```

:::

::: {}
```{python}
period_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Period":["Pre-COVID", "COVID Shock", "Post-Shock"],
    "Average Return":[pre["ReturnPct"].mean(), shock["ReturnPct"].mean(), post["ReturnPct"].mean()],
    "Volatility":[pre["ReturnPct"].std(), shock["ReturnPct"].std(), post["ReturnPct"].std()],
    "Anomaly Days":[
        df[df["Date"] < COVID_START]["Anomaly"].sum(),
        df[df["Date"].between(COVID_START, COVID_END)]["Anomaly"].sum(),
        df[df["Date"] > COVID_END]["Anomaly"].sum()
    ]
})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))
x = np.arange(len(period_summary))
w = 0.34
ax.bar(x-w/2, period_summary["Average Return"], width=w, color=TEAL, label="Average daily return")
ax.bar(x+w/2, period_summary["Volatility"], width=w, color=RED, label="Daily volatility")
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(period_summary["Period"])
ax.axhline(0, color=NAVY, linewidth=1.0)
ax.set_ylabel("Percent")
ax.set_title("COVID changed both return and risk", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.grid(axis="y")
for i, v in enumerate(period_summary["Anomaly Days"]):
    ax.text(i, max(period_summary["Volatility"].max(), period_summary["Average Return"].max())*0.85, f"{int(v)}\nanomaly\ndays", ha="center", color=NAVY, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

## 8. Forecasting Lesson and Final Takeaways

::: {.two-col}
::: {}

Forecasting after a shock is difficult because the future may not look like the past.

A simple forecast uses recent average return and recent volatility.

<div class="card card-orange" style="margin-bottom:12px;">
<strong>Key lesson:</strong> after COVID, uncertainty is as important as direction.
</div>

<div class="tk" style="margin-top:10px;">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#1A3A5C;"><span class="tk-n">01</span><span class="tk-t">Use returns, not just prices</span></div>
<div class="tk-b">Returns reveal gains, losses, risk, and market reaction.</div>
</div>

<div class="tk" style="margin-top:10px;">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#0D9488;"><span class="tk-n">02</span><span class="tk-t">Track rolling volatility</span></div>
<div class="tk-b">Volatility shows when the market becomes unpredictable.</div>
</div>

<div class="tk" style="margin-top:10px;">
<div class="tk-h" style="background:#1A3A5C;"><span class="tk-n">03</span><span class="tk-t">Flag anomalies early</span></div>
<div class="tk-b">Extreme days can trigger deeper business analysis and risk controls.</div>
</div>

:::

::: {}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
hist = df.tail(180)
ax.plot(hist["Date"], hist["Index100"], color=TEAL, linewidth=2.3, label="Historical index")
ax.plot(fc["Date"], fc["Forecast"], color=NAVY, linewidth=2.4, label="Simple forecast")
ax.fill_between(mdates.date2num(fc["Date"]), fc["Lower"].to_numpy(), fc["Upper"].to_numpy(), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.18, label="Uncertainty band")
ax.axvline(df["Date"].max(), color=GRAY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.4)
ax.grid(axis="y")
ax.set_ylabel("Index value")
ax.set_title("Simple forecast: direction plus uncertainty", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=NAVY)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

::: {.dark}
Final message: time series analysis helps marketing and analytics teams convert messy daily market data into a simple story about trend, risk, shock, and recovery.
:::
:::
